Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 50, verses 1–3:

Meccan [except verse 38, which is Medinan], and its verses are 45. [It was revealed after Surat al-Mursalat.] In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The discussion concerning Qaf. ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾, ﴿But they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves﴾ is similar to Sad: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾, ﴿Nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance﴾, equal to equal, because the two share one style. Al-Majid: possessing glory and nobility over other books. Whoever comprehends its meanings and acts by what is in it has glory with Allah and with people, and it is through a cause from Allah, the Glorious (al-Majid), so it is permissible for it to be described by His attribute.

As for His saying, ﴿But they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves﴾, it is a denial of their wondering at what is not wondrous: that a man from among them, whose intermediary role among them and whose justice and trustworthiness they know, should warn them of what is to be feared. Whoever is of such a description is only a sincere adviser to his people, ﴿hovering over them﴾ [[His saying "hovering over them" (mutarafrifan 'alayhim): in al-Sihah: "Fulan yarfudhuna" means he surrounds us and protects us. "Rafrafa al-ta'ir" means when a bird moves its wings around a thing, wanting to settle on it. "Raffa lawnuhu" with the letter fa' means raf and rafif: it shone and glittered. "Thawb rafif" and "shajar rafif" mean when its leaves are close together. Also in it: "tarqraqa al-shay'" with the letter qaf means it sparkled. (a)]], fearing that harm may befall them and something disagreeable may descend upon them. When he knows that a fearful thing has overshadowed them, it is incumbent upon him to warn them and caution them, so how much more so when it is the ultimate of fears and the end of what is to be avoided. It is also a denial of their wondering at what he warned them of, namely the Resurrection, despite their knowledge of Allah's power to create the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and to originate and bring into being everything, and their acknowledgment of the first creation, and despite the testimony of reason that there must be recompense. Then he relied on one of the two denials with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So the disbelievers said: This is a strange thing. When we die and become dust, [will we be returned?]﴾

It indicates that their wondering at the Resurrection is more entrenched in disbelief in its improbability and more deserving of denial. The word "the disbelievers" is placed in the position of the pronoun, as testimony that in this saying of theirs they are advancing into great disbelief. "This" refers to the return. "When" (idha) is governed by an implied verb, meaning: "When we die and decay, shall we return?" ﴿That is a far-off return﴾: improbable and denied, like your saying: "This is a distant saying," and "So-and-so has gone far in his saying," meaning far from imagination and custom. It is also permissible that "return" (raj') means "what is returned to" (al-marju'), which is the answer, and in that case it is part of Allah's speech, an expression of disapproval of their denial of what they were warned about, namely the Resurrection, and the pause before it according to this interpretation is good. It is also read "idha mitna" in the form of a statement, and its meaning is: "When we die after we return," and what indicates it is ﴿That is a far-off return﴾. If you ask: what governs the adverb when "return" means "what is returned to"? I answer: what the warner indicates from what he warned of, namely the Resurrection.

Qad ʿalimnā (We have indeed known) is a reply to their denial of resurrection (istibʿād al-rajʿ), because whoever's knowledge is so subtle that it penetrates to what the earth consumes of the bodies of the dead, eating their flesh and bones, is capable of returning them alive as they were. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every son of Adam decays, except the coccyx (ʿajb al-dhanb)" [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Abu Salih from Abu Hurayrah. Al-Hakim also narrated it from the hadith of Abu Saʿid, adding: "They said: 'What is it, O Messenger of God?' He said: 'It is like a mustard seed; from it they will be brought forth.'"]] And on the authority of al-Suddi: "What the earth diminishes of them" refers to whatever of them dies and is buried in the earth. ﴿A Book preserved﴾ means guarded from the devils and from alteration, and it is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz). Or it means one who preserves what has been entrusted to it and has recorded in it.

**Bal kadhdhabū** is an *idrab* (a turning away from a prior statement, meaning "rather"). It follows the first *idrab* to indicate that they have come up with something even more monstrous than their astonishment, namely denying the truth, which is prophethood established by miracles, at the very first moment, without reflection or contemplation. **Fahum fī amrin marīj**: confused, in turmoil. It is said: "The ring moved (*maraja*) on his finger and shook (*wa jaraja*)." They say at one time "a poet," at another "a sorcerer," and at another "a soothsayer," never holding firmly to one thing.

It is also read as **lammā jā'ahum** with the lām kasrah and *mā* as a verbal-noun particle (*mā al-maṣdariyya*). The lām here is the same as in their saying *lakhamsin khalaw* ("five had passed"), meaning: at the time of his coming to them. It is said that **bi'l-ḥaqq** refers to the Qur'an, and it is also said to refer to the report of resurrection.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 50, verse 6:

Have they not looked, when they disbelieved in the resurrection, at the signs of God's power in the creation of the world? ﴿We built it﴾: we raised it up. ﴿Without pillars﴾. ﴿Any cracks?﴾ Cracks, meaning fissures. He means that it is smooth and sound, free of defects, with no fissure, no split, and no flaw in it, like His saying, ﴿Do you see any flaw?﴾ (67:3).

We stretched it out (madadnāhā), spread it (daḥawnāhā), and placed upon it firm mountains (rawāsiya jibālan thawābit). And We cast upon it firm mountains lest it should shift (lawlā hiya li-takaffa'at), and from every pair (min kulli zawjin), of every kind (min kulli ṣinfin), a pleasing (bahīj), that delights by its beauty (yabtahij bihi li-ḥusnihi), as a insight (tabṣira) and a reminder (dhikrā), so that every servant who turns back (munīb), returning to his Lord, reflecting upon the wonders of His creation, may see by it (li-tabṣira bihi) and remember (wa-nadhkura).

It has also been read as tabṣiratan wa-dhikrā in the nominative (bi'l-raf'), meaning: He created them as an insight and a reminder.

Water that is blessed, abounding in benefits; and the grain of the harvest, the grain that is fit to be harvested, meaning that which people subsist upon, such as wheat, barley and others. Tall palm trees (باسِقاتٍ طوالا) in the sky. In the recitation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) it is read as باصقات, with the sin replaced by a sad because of the qaf. Layered upon one another (نَضِيدٌ منضود): bunched, one upon another. This may mean either the abundance of the spathes (ṭalʿ) and their piling up, or the abundance of the fruit within them. As sustenance (رِزْقاً), governed by "anbatnā-hā rizqan," because growing (al-inbāt) carries the sense of provision (al-rizq). Or it is a direct object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), meaning: We caused them to grow in order to provide for them. Thus is the Resurrection (كَذلِكَ الْخُرُوجُ): just as this dead land was brought to life, so will you be brought forth alive after your death. The kaf (كاف) here is in the nominative position, as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada').

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 50, verses 12–14:

He meant by Pharaoh his people, like His saying, ﴿from Pharaoh and their chiefs﴾, because the one coordinated before them is the people of Noah, and the coordinated items are groups. Each one may be meant individually, and it may be meant as all of them together, except that he made the pronoun referring to it singular according to the wording rather than the meaning. ﴿The word of punishment was realized﴾: it became obligatory, and My threat descended upon them, namely the word of punishment. In it there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and a warning to them.

﴿Was We wearied by the first creation?﴾ The verb ʿayiya bi-l-amr means to be unable to find the way to accomplish a task. The interrogative hamza (the hamzat al-inkar, the particle of denial) introduces the meaning: We were not unable to create the first creation, as they supposed, so that We would be unable to create the second. Then He said, ﴿Rather, they are in doubt about a new creation﴾. The phrase "then He said" should be understood as implying iḍrāb (a shift from one statement to another, correcting or redirecting the sense). The phrase "they do not deny" Our power to create the first creation, and their acknowledgment of that is, within it, an acknowledgment of the power to bring back the creation. ﴿Rather, they are in lubs (confusion), that is, in mixture and doubt.﴾

Satan has confused them and bewildered them. From this is the saying of ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him: "O Ḥārith, you are indeed confused. Know the truth, and you will know its people." The confusion of Satan over them is his embellishing to them that the revival of the dead is something outside the normal course, so they abandoned the sound analogy: whoever is able to originate is able to restore even more readily.

If you say: why did He make the new creation indefinite (nakira), and why did He not define it as He defined the first creation? I say: the definite form (taʿrīf) serves no purpose except to magnify and honour what is intended by it, as in the definiteness of "males" in His saying ﴿He bestows males on whom He wills﴾. For this purpose the first creation was defined, because the aim is to make it a proof of the possibility of the second creation by a stronger argument: that is, if Allah, Exalted is He, was not wearied by the first creation despite its greatness, then the later creation is even more deserving of not being regarded as burdensome. This is the secret of the definiteness of the first creation. As for indefiniteness (tankīr), its matter is divided. Sometimes it is intended to magnify the indefinite thing because of the vagueness it contains, as if it were too grand to be addressed as something known, as in ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾, and ﴿For them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾, and ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and bliss﴾, and ﴿We will join them with their offspring in faith﴾, and it is more than can be counted. Sometimes it is intended to diminish the indefinite thing and belittle it. The first is the more usual use of indefiniteness, so it does not need illustration. Thus the indefiniteness of "lubs" is for glorification and magnification, as if He said: "in confusion, what a confusion!" And the indefiniteness of "new creation" is to diminish it and make light of its matter in relation to the first creation. It may also be for magnification, as if it were a matter too great for a person to accept being confused about it, given that it is the first thing in which one should look for its soundness. Perhaps this is what al-Zamakhsharī intended, and Allah knows best. This, as you see, is a fitting discussion for the delight of questions and answers. If it is what al-Zamakhsharī meant, well and good; otherwise, "lick the honey and do not ask."

I answer: he intended, in making it indefinite, a new creation that has a great matter and a severe condition, so that whoever hears of it should be concerned about it, fear it, and investigate it, and not remain in confusion about such a thing.

The whisper (al-waswasa) is a hidden sound, as in the jingling of ornaments (wiswas al-hilī). The whispering of the soul (waswasat al-nafs) is what occurs to a person's mind and stirs in his conscience as inner speech. The preposition *bi-* in it is like your saying "he spoke with such-and-such" (ṣawwata bi-kadhā) and "he whispered it" (hamasa bihi). It is also permissible for the *bi-* to be transitive (al-ta'diya), with the pronoun referring to the human being, meaning: "what you make him whisper." The *mā* is then a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyya), because they say: "his soul spoke to him of such-and-such" (ḥaddatha nafsahu bi-kadhā), just as they say: "his soul spoke to him of it" (ḥaddathathu bihi nafsuhu). Someone said:

﻿"I lie to the soul when it speaks to me,
for the soul's truthfulness diminishes hope.
Only do not let it be truthful to you in piety,
and subdue it with righteousness, for God is the Greatest."

This is by Labīd ibn Rabīʿa. Bashshār was asked: "Which line of verse composed by the Arabs is the most poetic?" He said: "Preferring one line over all of poetry is not sound, but Labīd's is among the best in his saying: 'I lie to the soul.'" *Akdhib* ("I lie to") is said of *kadhdhaba* and *ṣaddaqa*, both lightened and intensified, with the same meaning. The *mā* here is from the first kind (i.e., the verb is in the first conjugation) for the metre's sake. That is: do not believe it when it speaks to you of a matter and it speaks to you about it, because it discourages you from attaining virtues and aspires toward vices. This is the meaning of "if the soul is truthful," that is, its being believed, "diminishes hope." It is said: *zarāhu* when he blamed him, and *azrā bihi* when he brought blame upon him. The word *ghayr* here is an accusative of circumstance (ḥāl), meaning: "the matter and the situation: do not lie to it when it speaks to you of piety and fear of God." *Inna* is here a lightened form of the heavy particle (mukhaffafa min al-thaqīla), and its noun is a dummy pronoun (ḍamīr al-sha'n). It is also permissible that it is the pronoun of the addressee, and *lā* is a prohibitive particle. Arranging the sentence as an exception requires some effort in identifying the excepted and the excepted-from; it can be arranged as a correction (istidrāk), but the accusative of *ghayr* then requires taking it as an exception. It is also possible that *an* is a verbal-source particle and *lā* is a negation or an extra particle, but emphasizing the verb with the *nūn* is common after a prohibition, rare after a negation, and anomalous or poetic-licence with an affirmative. The sentence must be arranged in this manner as an exception, in meaning and in wording.

Al-Qasṭallānī said in his commentary on Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī that it allows the prohibitive reading and the extra-particle reading. Some of them allow the negative reading, based on the Prophet's words (ﷺ) to ʿĀʾisha when she menstruated during the Ḥajj: "Do what the pilgrim does, except that you do not circumambulate the House." *Khazāhu yakhzūhu* means: he subdued him and overcame him. That is: subdue it with goodness to God, the Greatest, the Supreme. It seems that in righteousness there is a kind of subjugation of it, because it is generally burdensome to it.

"And We are nearer to him" (﴿وَنَحْنُ أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْهِ﴾) is a metaphor (majāz). The intended meaning is the nearness of His knowledge to him, that His knowledge is connected to what is known about him and about his states in a way that nothing of its hidden aspects escapes Him. It is as if His essence were near him, as one says: "God is in every place," though He is exalted above places. "The jugular vein" (ḥabl al-warīd) is a figure for extreme nearness, like their saying: "he is more present to me than the midwife's seat and the knot of my waistwrap." Dhū al-Rumma said:

﻿"Shall I live in a pleasant, luxurious life,
while death is nearer to me than the jugular?"

This is by Dhū al-Rumma. The interrogative is one of denial, meaning: I shall not live a wide life while death is nearer to me than the jugular. It is also transmitted as *awfā* ("more so"), and the meaning is the same. The *warīdān* are two veins at the front of the two sides of the neck; they were named so because they bring (yaridāni) blood from the head. And he said "pleasant" (raghīd) in the same way as God's words: "Indeed, the mercy of God is near (qarīb)," although it is in the form *faʿīl* in the sense of *fāʿil*.

The *ḥabl* is the vein, likened to a single rope (wāḥid al-ḥibāl). Do you not see his saying:

﻿"As if his two jugulars were a rope of a well-bucket,
a lion of the thicket at the moment of anger."

This is by Ru'ba. *Ghaḍanfar* is the lion. The two *warīdān* are the two veins that come from the head and enclose the windpipe. It is said that the spirit brings them (tarudduhumā).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 50, verses 19–22:

When He mentioned their denial of the Resurrection and argued against them by describing His power and knowledge, He informed them that what they had denied and rejected would befall them soon, at their death and at the establishment of the Hour. He drew attention to the nearness of this by expressing it in the past tense, in His words ﴿And the agony of death will have come with the truth﴾, and [﴿and the Horn will be blown﴾]. "Sakrat al-mawt" (the agony of death) means its severe intensity that takes away the intellect.

The bāʾ in "bil-ḥaqq" (with the truth) is for ta'diyah (making the verb transitive, i.e. the bāʾ marks the object brought). The meaning is: the agony of death has brought into presence the reality that Allah revealed in His books and sent His messengers with. Or it means the reality and the clear state of affairs: the happiness or wretchedness of the dying person. It was also said: the truth for which man was created, namely that every soul will taste death.

The bāʾ may also be like its use in His words ﴿grows with the oil﴾ (tanbutu bil-duhn), meaning "came in a state of being joined with the truth", i.e. with the reality of the matter, or with wisdom and a correct purpose, like His words ﴿He created the heavens and the earth with the truth﴾.

Abu Bakr and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both, read: "sakrat al-ḥaqq bil-mawt" (the agony of the truth with death), with the agony annexed to the truth (idafah), indicating that it is the agony that was prescribed for man and made obligatory upon him, and that it is wisdom. The bāʾ is for ta'diyah, because it is the cause of the departure of the soul through its severity, or because death follows it, so that it is as if it came with it. It is also possible that the meaning is: it came and death was with it. It was also said: "sakrat al-ḥaqq" is the agony of Allah, annexed to Him to magnify its matter and make it terrifying.

It was read: "sakarat al-mawt" (the agonies of death).

"Dhālika" (that) is a reference to death. The address to man in His words ﴿And We have certainly created man﴾ is by way of iltifāt (a shift of grammatical person). Or it refers to the truth, and the address is to the wicked.

"Taḥīd" means to shy away and flee.

It is reported from some of them that he asked Zayd ibn Aslam about this, and he said: the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He related this to Salih ibn Kaysan, who said: By Allah, this is not the way of an eloquent style, nor of a fluent tongue, nor of knowledge of the speech of the Arabs; it is addressed to the disbelievers. Then he related both views to al-Husayn ibn Abd Allah ibn Ubayd Allah ibn Abbas, who said: I disagree with both of them: it is addressed to the righteous and the wicked alike.

﴿That is the Day of the Promised Threat﴾: this is on the supposition that a noun has been omitted, i.e. "the time of that is the Day of the Promised Threat", and the reference is to the source of "the Horn" (al-nafkh).

﴿A driver and a witness﴾: two angels, one of whom drives him to the place of gathering, and the other testifies against him for his deeds. Or it is one angel who combines both functions, as if it were said: with it is an angel who drives it and bears witness against it.

The position of ﴿with it, a driver﴾ (maʿahā sāʾiq) is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from "kull" (every soul), because it is made definite by the idafah (annexation) to what is in the position of a definite noun.

It was read: "Laqad kunta" (you were certainly). ﴿We have removed from you your covering, so your sight today is sharp﴾, with a kasra on the kāf in "kunta" as address to the soul, i.e. it will be said to it: "Laqad kunta (you were certainly)...". Heedlessness was made as if it were a covering with which the whole body is covered, or a veil with which the eyes are covered, so that it sees nothing. When the Day of Resurrection comes, he awakens, heedlessness and its covering are removed from him, and he sees what he did not see of the truth. "And his eyes returned, dull (kalīl) from seeing because of his heedlessness": ḥadīd (sharp) because of his alertness.

If you ask: what is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of this statement? I answer:

If you make mā (ما) a qualifying noun (mawṣūfah, i.e., indefinite "a thing"), then ʿatīd is an adjective (ṣifah) describing it. If you make it a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), then ʿatīd is either a substitute (badal), or a predicate following another predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada').

"Alqiyā" (throw, both of you) is an address from God Most High to the two angels mentioned earlier: the driver (al-sāʾiq) and the witness (al-shahīd). It is permissible for it to be an address to a single person, in two ways.

The first is the view of al-Mubarrad: the dual form of the agent was placed in the position of the dual form of the verb, because the two are united in purpose, as if it were said: "Alqi, alqi" (throw, throw), for emphasis.

**Question:** Why was this sentence left without the conjunction *wa* (and), while the first one was joined to what precedes it?

**Answer:** Because it is a resumed sentence (*istinaf*), just as the sentences in a report of a back-and-forth exchange are resumed, as you have seen in the account of the dialogue between Musa and Fir'awn (Pharaoh).

**Question:** Then where is the back-and-forth exchange here?

**Answer:** When his companion said ﴿This is what is with me, ready﴾, and this was followed by ﴿His companion said: "Our Lord, I did not make him rebellious"﴾, and then by ﴿Do not dispute in My presence﴾, it became known that there was an exchange from the disbeliever, but it was omitted because what indicates it is present. It is as if he said: "My Lord, he made me rebellious," and then his companion said: "Our Lord, I did not make him rebellious."

As for the first sentence, it must be joined by conjunction, to indicate that its meaning and the meaning of what precedes it occur together, namely the coming of every soul with the two angels. The companion's statement, "I did not make him rebellious," means: I did not make him a rebel, and I did not cause him to fall into rebellion, but he rebelled and chose misguidance over guidance, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿I had no authority over you, except that I called you and you responded to me﴾.

He said: "Do not dispute before Me, when I had already sent forward to you the warning."

Note: this is a continuation (istinaf) like His saying "His companion said..." as if someone asked, "What did Allah say?" and it was answered: He said, "Do not dispute." The meaning: do not dispute in the abode of recompense and the place of reckoning, for there is no benefit in your disputing and no outcome from it. I had already threatened you with My punishment for transgression in My Books and through the tongues of My messengers, so I left you no argument against Me. Then He said: do not hope that I will change My word or My threat so that I pardon you from what I threatened you with, "and I am not unjust to the servants," so that I would punish one who does not deserve punishment.

Or it is transitive (muʿaddiyah), with qaddama (to send forward) being an intransitive-form verb in the sense of taqaddama (to go forward). It is also permissible that the verb governs the clause "what is changed of the word with Me, and I am not unjust to the servants," and that "bil-waʿid" is a circumstantial (hal), meaning: "I have sent this forward to you, accompanied by the threat, joined with it," or "I have sent it forward to you as a promise to you through it."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 50, verse 30:

It is recited as "naqūlu" (with nūn) and as "yaqūlu" (with yā'). It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "On the day Allah says to Jahannam..." And it is related from Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan: "yuqāl" (it is said). The accusative of "al-yawm" (the day) is governed either by "ẓalām" (darkness), or by an implied verb, like "udhkur" (remember) and "undhir" (warn). It is also permissible for it to be governed by "nafkh" (the blowing), as if it were said: "And the Trumpet is blown on the day We say to Jahannam..." On this reading, "dhālika" (that) points to "the day We say," and there is no need to posit an omitted noun (muḍāf). The questioning of Jahannam and its answer is of the category of takhyīl (imaginative representation) [[Mahmud said: "The questioning of Jahannam and its answer is of the category of takhyīl, by which is intended the depiction of the meaning..." etc. Ahmad said: My earlier objection to his use of the term takhyīl in more than one place has already been stated, and the objection here is stronger, for the term takhyīl has already appeared in his usage in such a statement as "and the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection," and in such a statement as "rather, both His hands are outstretched." He intended by it the interpretation of the hands as a kind of metaphor. The meaning of his words is sound, for we hold that these two are metaphorical, and we profess Allah's exaltation above the literal understanding, so there is no harm in its general sense. Yet we are addressed to avoid expressions that give rise to misconception concerning the majesty of Allah, even if their meanings are correct, and what misconception is greater than the misconception of the word takhyīl? Do you not see how Allah used it regarding what He reported to be magic and falsehood, in His saying: "It is imagined to him from their magic that it runs" — so there can be no doubt of the obligation to avoid it. Then our discussion returns to its use here, and we say: it is objectionable both in wording and in meaning.

As for the wording, it has already been mentioned. As for the meaning, we hold that the questioning of Jahannam and its answer are literal, and that Allah creates in it the perception for that, under its condition. And how could we posit otherwise, when reports have come and are mutually reinforcing on this: among them this one; and among them the disputation of Paradise and the Fire; and among them Jahannam's complaint to its Lord, whereupon He permitted it two breaths. Although these are not explicit texts, they are apparent indications that must be taken in their literal sense, for we are obliged to believe the apparent meaning unless an impediment prevents it, and there is no impediment here: the power is capable, reason permits it, and the apparent texts require the occurrence of what reason depicts. Something of this sort has certainly occurred in this world, such as the greeting of the trees and the glorification of the pebbles in the palm of the Prophet (ﷺ) and in the hands of his companions. Had the door of metaphor been opened, and departure from apparent meanings in the details of the discourse, the gap would have been impossible to close, and many people would have strayed from the truth. This is not like the apparent texts concerning divine attributes whose apparent meaning reason does not permit us to believe, for departing from the apparent sense there is a necessity imposed by the rational proofs that guide to the correct belief. So hold firmly, with what this section has detailed, to what I have pointed you to as the path of nearness and connection, and Allah is the Granter of success.]] which is intended to depict the meaning in the heart and to fix it. In it there are two meanings. The first: it fills up despite its vastness and the distance of its extremities, so that nothing can contain it [[His words "so that nothing can contain it" seem to contain an inversion. (Ṣ)]] and nothing more can be added to its filling, according to His saying: "I will certainly fill Jahannam." The second: it is so spacious that whoever enters it enters, and there is still room for more. It is permissible that "hal min mazīd" (Is there any more?) is an expression of astonishment at those who enter it and of deeming an increase unlikely upon them, because of their great number; or a request for more, out of rage against the disobedient. And "al-mazīd" is either a verbal noun like "al-maḥīd" and "al-mamīd," or a passive participle like "al-mabīʿ."

**"Not far off"** is in the accusative as an adverb of place (*zarf*), meaning: a place not far off. It may also be a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). It is masculine in form because it follows the pattern of a verbal noun (*masdar*), like *za'ir* (roaring) and *sahil* (clanging), and verbal nouns used as descriptors are the same for masculine and feminine. It may also be taken as an accusative of an omitted qualified noun (*mawsuf*), meaning: "something not far off." Its function here is emphasis (*tawkid*), as in your saying, "He is near, not distant," or "mighty, not humbled."

It is also read as *tu'adūn* with the *ta'* and with the *ya'*. In that reading it is a parenthetical clause (*jumla i'tiradiyya*).

**"For every penitent (*awwab*) [who is] watchful"** is an apposition (*badal*) of "for the God-fearing" in the previous verse, with the preposition repeated, as in God's words ﴿to those who were deemed weak, to those among them who believed﴾. This refers to the reward, or to the noun of the verb *uzlifat* (was brought near).

The *awwab* is one who returns repeatedly to the remembrance of God, and the *hafiz* is one who guards His limits.

**"Who feared the Merciful in secret"** is a second apposition following the first apposition, governed by *li-kull*. It may also be an apposition of the adjectives *awwab* and *hafiz*. It cannot, however, be in the same position as *awwab* and *hafiz*, because *man* (who) is not described by such a word, and among relative pronouns it is described only by *alladhi* (the one who), alone. It may also be the subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is "It will be said to them, 'Enter it in peace,'" because *man* carries the sense of the plural. It may also be a vocative (*munada*), as in the saying, "Whoever keeps doing good, do good to me," with the vocative particle omitted for closeness.

**"In secret"** is a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) of the object: he feared Him while He was unseen, whom he had not known, and whose punishing him was known only through inference. Or it is a qualifier of the verbal noun of *khashiya* (feared), meaning: he feared Him with a fear mixed with the unseen, in that he feared His punishment while He was absent, or he feared Him because of the unseen threat He made of His punishment. It was also said: in privacy, where no one sees him.

If you ask: how did He link fear with His name that signifies the vastness of mercy? I say: for the high praise of the one who fears, which is his fear, while knowing that He is vast in mercy, just as He praised him as one who fears, even though the one feared is unseen. Similar is God's words ﴿and those who give what they give while their hearts tremble﴾, where He described them with trembling despite their abundant acts of obedience.

The heart is described with *inaba* (turning back), which is returning to God, because what counts is what is firmly established in the heart.

**"It will be said to them, 'Enter it in peace'"** means: safe from punishment and from the loss of blessings.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 50, verse 37:**

﴿For whoever has a heart﴾: that is, a heart that is attentive, because one whose heart does not pay attention is as though he had no heart. "And gives ear" (*ilqa' al-sam'*): that is, listens (*al-isgha'*). ﴿And he is a witness﴾: that is, present with his understanding, because one whose mind is not present is as though he were absent. Imam Abd al-Qahir (al-Jurjani) made a witty remark to one of those who took knowledge from him:

*"Whatever you wish of zahzahah, while the young man is at Musaqlabad, [watering] crops.
He comes in a spare moment of his time, like one whose passion has been mixed with longing (al-nuz'a).
Then you see a stubborn, fiery-natured one, whose loads have been bound tight with ropes (al-nusu')."*

*"Whatever you wish of zahzahah, while the young man is at Musaqlabad, [watering] crops."*

He alluded to this in the case of one of those who took from him but whose mind was not present, namely Abu Amir al-Jurjani. That is: he comes in the remainder of his time, while his thought is attached to something other than what has brought him, like one who has mixed passion with *al-nuz'a*, meaning return; *al-nuz'a* is also used for longing. Then he sees a coarse nature and disposition, kindled with the passions of youth. *Al-jibla* (with two kasras, then shaddah, and also with the first letter having three vowel forms and the second sukun) means creation and disposition, and it is probably construed with what follows it in the manner of a noun construed with its adjective. It is said: *shabba yashibbu wa yashubbu shababan wa shabiyyan*, meaning he put on a shirt and played. *Shabbabtu al-nar shabban wa shububan*, meaning I kindled the fire. *Shabbabtuhu*, meaning I made it manifest. *Ashbabtuhu*, meaning I excited it.

It is also narrated as:

*"Then you see a sitter in haste (mustawfiz)"*, that is, hastening, prepared to rise. This version is more suitable in meter and meaning. *Al-nasa'* is a wide strap placed beneath the chest of a riding beast, the covering of a howdah, the slackening of the flesh of the gums, the north wind, departure, and rapid growth of plants. Its plural is *ansa'*, *nusu'* and *nus'*. That is: the state is that its loads have been bound with ropes, as a metaphor for departure.

The Persian, when approving of a matter, says *zahazah*, and from it the word *zahzahah* is taken. That is: whatever approval you wish during learning is found in him in abundance. The address is to someone unspecified. The state is that the young man is at Musaqlabad, which is a quarter in Jurjan. It is narrated with a dhal with a dot (*Musaqladhabad*), meaning he is there watering his crops. Since his heart is attached only to that place, his body is as though it were there. He has advanced in the simile: he compared him to one who has mixed passion with something else, as an eloquent simile; then to one who has prepared himself to depart, as an illustration; then to one who has actually traveled, reached his destination and occupied himself with what is there, as an eloquent simile. How excellent his eloquence is!

Or: ﴿and he is a witness﴾ means he is a witness to its truth and that it is revelation from God. Or it means he is one of the witnesses in the Almighty's words, ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾. And it is narrated from Qatadah that it means he is a witness to its truth from among the People of the Book, because its description is present with him.

Al-Suddi and a group read *alqa al-sam'* in the passive form, meaning: for whoever has had his hearing given to another, and his ear opened to him, and yet his mind is not present, while he is present-minded and attentive. It is also said: *alqa sam'ahu*, or *al-sam'* from him.

Al-lughūb: fatigue, exhaustion (al-i'yā'). It is also read with a fatḥah (lughab), on the pattern of qabūl and walū'.

It is said: it was revealed concerning the Jews, refuting their claim that God created the heavens and the earth in six days, the first of which was Sunday and the last Friday, and that He rested on Saturday and reclined upon the Throne. They also said: the anthropomorphism (al-tashbīh) that occurred in this community came only from the Jews, and from them it was taken.

فَاصْبِرْ عَلى ما يَقُولُونَ ﴿فاصبر على ما يقولون﴾: أي اليهود، وما يأتون به من الكفر والتشبيه (*tashbih*، أي تشبيه الله بخلقه). وقيل: فاصبر على ما يقول المشركون من إنكارهم البعث، فإنّ من قدر على خلق العالم قدر على بعثهم والانتقام منهم. وقيل: هي منسوخة بآية السيف (*naskh*، أي النسخ، وهو رفع حكم بدليل شرعي متأخر). وقيل: الصبر مأمور به في كل حال.

﴿بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ﴾: حامدا ربك. والتسبيح محمول على ظاهره، أو على الصلاة. فالصلاة ﴿قَبْلَ طُلُوعِ الشَّمْسِ﴾: الفجر. ﴿وَقَبْلَ الْغُرُوبِ﴾: الظهر والعصر. ﴿وَمِنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾: العشاءان. وقيل: التهجد. ﴿وَأَدْبارَ السُّجُودِ﴾: التسبيح في آثار الصلوات، والسجود والركوع يعبر بهما عن الصلاة. وقيل: النوافل بعد المكتوبات (الفرائض). وعن علي رضي الله عنه: الركعتان بعد المغرب. وروي عن النبي ﷺ: «من صلى بعد المغرب قبل أن يتكلم كتبت صلاته في عليين» (*illiyyin*، وهو المكان الرفيع في السماء) [[أخرجه ابن أبي شيبة وعبد الرزاق من رواية عبد العزيز بن عمر: سمعت مكحولا يقول: بلغني أن النبي ﷺ قال «من صلى ركعتين بعد المغرب قبل أن يتكلم كتبتا- أو قال رفعتا- في عليين» هذا مرسل. وقد روي موصولا عن أنس عن عائشة رضي الله عنهما. أما حديث أنس فرواه الدارقطني في غرائب مالك، من رواية أحمد بن سليمان الأسدي عنه عن الزهري عن أنس به وأتم منه. وقال: هذا موضوع على مالك. وأما حديث عائشة فرواه ابن شاهين في الترغيب. وفي إسناده جعفر بن جميع]]. وعن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما: الوتر بعد العشاء.

والأدبار: جمع دبر. وقرئ: ﴿وَإِدْبارَ السُّجُودِ﴾ بكسر الهمزة، من أدبرت الصلاة إذا انقضت وتمت. ومعناه: ووقت انقضاء السجود، كقولهم: آتيك خفوق النجم.

﴿وَاسْتَمِعْ﴾: أي استمع لما أخبرك به من حال يوم القيامة. وفي ذلك تهويل وتعظيم لشأن المخبر به والمحدَّث عنه، كما يروى عن النبي ﷺ أنه قال لمعاذ بن جبل سبعة أيام: «يا معاذ اسمع ما أقول لك»، ثم حدثه بعد ذلك [[لم أجده.]].

فإن قلت: بمَ انتصب اليوم؟ قلت: بما دل عليه ﴿ذلِكَ يَوْمُ الْخُرُوجِ﴾، أي: يوم ينادي المنادي فيخرجون من القبور. ﴿يَوْمَ يَسْمَعُونَ الصَّيْحَةَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ بدل من ﴿يَوْمَ يُنادِ الْمُنادِ﴾. والمنادي إسرافيل ينفخ في الصور وينادي: أيتها العظام البالية، والأوصال المنقطعة، واللحوم المتمزقة، والشعور المتفرقة، إنّ الله يأمركن أن تجتمعن لفصل القضاء.

وقيل: إسرافيل ينفخ، وجبريل ينادي بالحشر. ﴿مِنْ مَكانٍ قَرِيبٍ﴾: من صخرة بيت المقدس، وهي أقرب الأرض من السماء باثني عشر ميلا، وهي وسط الأرض. وقيل: من تحت أقدامهم. وقيل: من منابت شعورهم، يسمع من كل شعرة: أيتها العظام البالية.

﴿وَالصَّيْحَةَ﴾: النفخة الثانية. ﴿بِالْحَقِّ﴾: متعلق بالصيحة، والمراد به البعث والحشر للجزاء.

And it is read as *tashaqqaq*, and as *tashaqqaq* with the *ta'* assimilated into the *shin* (*idghām*, the merging of one letter into the next), and as *tushaqqaq* in the passive form, and *tanshaqqu* *sirā'an*. *Sirā'an* is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*, a word expressing the state of the subject or object) from the object pronoun in *ʿalaynā*. The fronting of the adverbial phrase *ʿalaynā* (*taqdīm al-ẓarf*) indicates exclusivity: *yasīr* means that such a tremendous matter is made easy only for the Capable, the Essential One, whom no affair distracts from another affair. As He, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only like that of a single soul﴾.

We know best what they say. It is a threat to them and consolation to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). ﴿Not a compeller﴾ over them, like His saying, ﴿You are not over them a dictator﴾ (bi-musaytir), so that you would force them to belief. ﴿You are only one who calls and one who rouses﴾ [[His saying "you are only one who calls and one who rouses," meaning: you rouse people to belief. (ʿA.)]]. It was also said: what is meant is forbearance toward them and abandoning harshness against them. It is also permissible that it derives from "jabara" in the sense of "compelled him to the matter" (ajbarahu ʿalayhi), meaning: you are not one who governs over them, forcing them to belief. ʿAla here has the same function as in your saying "he is over them" when he is their governor and the one who holds their affairs. ﴿Those who fear My warning﴾, like His saying, ﴿You are only a warner to one who fears it﴾, because it benefits only those (who fear), not the one who persists in disbelief.
